Class For

java.lang.Object
forj.For
public final class For extends Object
What forj comprehensions compile to. The plugin rewrites 
forj {                       forj.For.run(() -> forjLower(
    x <- xs;                     forj.For.forjFlatMap(forjLift(xs), x ->
    guard(p(x));      ==>            forj.For.forjMap(forj.For.forjFilter(forjLift(ys(x)), y -> p(x)),
    y <- ys(x);                          y -> f(x, y)))))
} yield f(x, y);
(guards filter the generator they follow) and passes each combinator its type class instance at compile time: a comprehension over F needs a Monad<F> (Functor<F> for a single generator, plus FunctorFilter<F> for guards). Generic code (<F> ... using Monad<F> m) works the same way as concrete types.

Lifting

forjLift turns a generator's value into a Kind and is called unqualified, so overloads from any import static take part. forjLower turns the result back, through the Lower method for the witness. A library adds a type by shipping a forjLift overload, a @Lower method and a given Monad<ItsType>. Types that already are a Kind (like IO) need none of the first two. This class is imported automatically into files that use forj.

    • forjLower

      public static <F, A, K extends Kind<F,A>> K forjLower(Kind<F,A> fa)
      Turns a comprehension's result back into a plain type. Written for types that are their own Kind (like IO) and for generic F: the target type must be a Kind<F, A>, so a wrong yield type is a compile error. For witnesses with an Lower method the plugin calls that instead, e.g. lowerList(Kind).
